chapterName: Middle Republic: Rome Turns East (200-167 BCE)

questions.question: Which fortresses were known as the "fetters of Greece"? (select all that apply)
options: Demetrias
Chalcis
Pella
Ephesus
Corinth
questions.explanation: Whoever held Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias could control Greece, and Rome kept troops in all three. The legions did not fully leave until 194 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Rome kept troops in Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, three fortresses known as the "fetters of Greece" because whoever held them could control the country.

questions.question: What new demand did Flamininus make of Philip V, beyond simply stopping attacks on Greek cities?
options: Withdraw garrisons from everywhere beyond Macedon, even Thessaly
Pay Rome's costs for the entire war
Surrender his war elephants and his whole navy
Hand over his eldest son as a hostage to Rome
Break off his secret pact with Antiochus III
questions.explanation: Flamininus demanded compensation for every harmed city and withdrawal from everywhere beyond Macedon, including Thessaly. Philip stormed out of the meeting.
questions.sourceQuote: Flamininus raised the price: Philip must compensate every city he had harmed and pull his garrisons out of everywhere beyond Macedon, even Thessaly, the broad plain of north-central Greece that Macedon had held since 353 BC.

questions.question: According to ancient writers, why did the peace talks of winter 198 BC go nowhere?
options: Philip's envoys were murdered on the way to Rome
Flamininus was waiting to learn whether his command would be extended
Philip refused to give up Thessaly under any terms
Antiochus III threatened to invade if Philip made peace
The Senate had already ordered a final campaign
questions.explanation: Ancient writers claimed Flamininus wanted a quick peace only if he was to be replaced. Once he learned his command would be extended, his friends in Rome quietly sank the deal.
questions.sourceQuote: Elections were under way in Rome, and Flamininus did not yet know whether his command would be extended (*prorogatio*).

questions.question: Why did the Centuriate Assembly at first reject war with Philip V in 200 BC?
options: Anger at Athens for refusing to pay troops
Fear of Philip's alliance with Antiochus III
Exhaustion after years of fighting Carthage
Omens declared the war unlucky
A tribune vetoed the consul's proposal
questions.explanation: The almost unanimous and unprecedented refusal was blamed on war-weariness after the Second Punic War. At a second meeting the consul changed their minds.
questions.sourceQuote: It refused almost unanimously, an unprecedented rejection blamed on exhaustion after years of fighting Carthage.

questions.question: What became of the great Carthaginian general at Antiochus III's court after Apamea?
options: He returned to Carthage and led it in a new war
He was handed to Rome and executed in the Forum
He retired peacefully on the island of Rhodes
He fled and years later killed himself rather than be surrendered
He was sent to Rome as one of the twenty hostages
questions.explanation: Antiochus was required to hand over Rome's enemies, but the general fled. Years later he took his own life rather than be surrendered.
questions.sourceQuote: The great Carthaginian general at his court fled instead, and years later killed himself rather than be surrendered.

questions.question: Ancient accounts of how the Battle of Pydna began disagree. What does the version favoured by the Roman historian who told it at greatest length say?
options: Aemilius drove a riderless horse toward the enemy
A Roman officer challenged a Macedonian to single combat
A mule broke loose at a river and a scuffle over it grew
Perseus attacked during the lunar eclipse
The Macedonians charged at dawn after a feast
questions.explanation: In this humbler version, a runaway mule sparked a scuffle while both sides drew water, and the armies poured in. Other writers said Aemilius provoked the battle with a riderless horse.
questions.sourceQuote: The version favoured by the Roman historian who told the story at greatest length is humbler: a mule broke loose while both sides were drawing water from a river, a scuffle over it grew, and both armies poured in.

questions.question: How much tribute did each of the four Macedonian republics have to pay Rome?
options: Double what the king had taken
Half what the king had taken
Nothing at all
One-tenth of their harvests
The same as the king had taken
questions.explanation: Each republic paid Rome half what the king had collected. The republics were centred on Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia.
questions.sourceQuote: It was split into four republics, centred on Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia, each paying Rome a tribute (*tributum*) half what the king had taken.

questions.question: At which great shrine was the king of Pergamon nearly murdered, in a plot blamed on Perseus?
options: Delphi
Olympia
Dodona
Samothrace
Delos
questions.explanation: The near-murder at Delphi, the shrine of Apollo, came soon after the king accused Perseus in Rome. Rome then declared Perseus a public enemy, and war began in 171 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Soon afterwards that king was nearly murdered on a visit to Delphi, the great shrine of Apollo, and the plot was blamed on Perseus.

questions.question: What happened near the hill of Callinicus in Thessaly early in the war with Perseus?
options: Perseus surrendered his treasury to a Roman fleet
Roman troops mutinied and demanded to go home
The Romans crushed Perseus's phalanx in under an hour
The Aetolians switched sides to join Perseus
Perseus's cavalry and light troops won a clear victory over Rome
questions.explanation: Perseus killed 2,000 Roman infantry and 200 cavalry for small losses. Even so, Rome answered his peace offers by demanding total surrender.
questions.sourceQuote: Near a hill called Callinicus in Thessaly, Perseus's cavalry and light troops won a clear victory, killing 2,000 Roman infantry and 200 cavalry for small losses of their own.

questions.question: Who did Philip V call up for the army that fought at Cynoscephalae?
options: A small elite guard of 5,000 picked men
Only professional mercenaries from Crete and Gaul
Conscripts from the Greek cities he had seized
Every man he could spare, from aged veterans to underage boys
Soldiers lent to him by Antiochus III
questions.explanation: Philip scraped together about 18,000 Macedonians, from old veterans to boys. Thracian light troops and hired soldiers fought alongside them.
questions.sourceQuote: Philip now called up every man his kingdom could spare, from aged veterans to underage boys: about 18,000 Macedonians, plus Thracian light troops and hired soldiers.
